# Introduction

- Anderson and Gerbing (1988): guidance for using SEM to test theory
- Main idea → check measurement first, then relationships between constructs
- Observed indicators = things like survey responses; latent constructs = ideas like trust or satisfaction
- Measurement model: do the items measure the intended construct?
- Structural model: do the proposed relationships between constructs hold up?

# Background

## Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

- Exploratory → look for possible factor structure
- Confirmatory → start with a structure based on theory, then check fit
- More of a progression; revising a confirmatory model adds an exploratory part
- Changes based on the same sample can pick up sample-specific patterns
- Stronger check: test the revised model with a new sample

## Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

- Theory testing: ML or GLS with a common-factor model
- Common-factor approach → separate measurement error from the construct; test overall fit
- Prediction: authors discuss PLS, emphasizing explained variance and component scores
- Choice depends on the research goal
- Article mainly focused on ML/GLS for confirmatory theory testing

## Estimation Methods

- ML → estimate parameters that reproduce the observed covariance patterns
- Distribution assumptions matter for standard errors and chi-square tests
- Parameter estimates may hold up better than the tests under moderate nonnormality
- Alternatives for nonnormal data available, but larger samples may be needed
- Fit results depend partly on the data and estimation method

# Confirmatory Measurement Model

- Specify which indicators belong to each latent construct
- Constructs allowed to correlate freely; proposed structural paths come later
- Each indicator includes error → survey responses are imperfect measures

## Need for Unidimensional Measurement

- Unidimensionality → one underlying idea measured by a set of indicators
- Several ideas mixed together = unclear construct meaning
- Internal consistency: relationships among items within a set
- External consistency: how those items relate to indicators outside the set
- Clear measurement needed before interpreting relationships between constructs

## Specification

- Decide indicator-to-construct relationships in advance using theory and item meaning
- Identification → enough information to estimate the parameters
- Consider scale setting, number of indicators, and measurement errors
- Cross-loadings/correlated errors need a reason; can change the construct's meaning

## Assessment of Fit

- Chi-square → compare model-predicted covariances with observed covariances
- Also check other fit information; chi-square sensitive to sample size
- Residuals → relationships the model explains poorly
- Check loadings, standard errors, and whether estimates make sense
- Convergent validity → indicators of the same construct come together
- Discriminant validity → different constructs can be distinguished
- Good overall fit alone doesn't guarantee good measurement

## Respecification

- Weak fit → inspect items, residuals, and theory before making changes
- Possible changes: remove weak indicator or rethink a specified relationship
- Chasing better statistics can overfit the sample
- Revisions need a theoretical reason; test with new data when possible
- Fix measurement first so structural paths aren't covering up item problems

# One-Step Versus Two-Step Modeling Approaches

## The Confirmatory Structural Model

- Add proposed relationships among latent constructs
- Example: awareness → intention to visit
- Theory places restrictions on which paths are included
- Interpretational confounding → construct meaning shifts when structural paths change
- Watch for noticeable changes in indicator loadings across structural models

## Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach

### Step 1: Measurement Model

- Check whether indicators measure the intended constructs
- Let constructs correlate freely; don't impose theoretical paths yet
- Check unidimensionality, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and fit
- Poor fit → examine measurement choices and make defensible revisions
- Need acceptable measurement before testing the structural theory

### Step 2: Structural Model

- Keep the established measurement structure; estimate the full model with proposed paths
- Test restrictions on relationships between constructs
- Compare fit with the freely correlated measurement model
- Nomological validity → constructs relate as expected within the theory
- Bad measurement would make these path results hard to interpret

### Nested Models and Difference Tests

- Nested models → more restricted model's free parameters are a subset of the less restricted model's
- Authors compare a series: null, more constrained alternative, proposed theory, less constrained alternative, and saturated structural model
- Saturated structural model equivalent to the freely correlated measurement model
- Chi-square difference test → difference in chi-square values, using difference in degrees of freedom
- Sequential tests → check whether added restrictions significantly worsen fit
- Main question: does the proposed theory explain construct relationships well enough? Does a reasonable alternative do better?

## Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

- Easier to locate poor fit → measurement problem vs. structural-path problem
- Good fit in one part can't hide poor fit in the other
- Less interpretational confounding → construct meaning more stable across models
- Clear baseline for comparing the theory with alternatives
- Missing paths also provide theoretical information
- Adding every possible path may improve fit but weakens the theory test


# Conclusion

- Main takeaway → define and check constructs before interpreting their relationships
- Measurement quality affects the meaning of structural paths
- Two steps: acceptable measurement → test theory → compare alternatives
- Fit statistics help, but theory and careful interpretation still needed

# References

Anderson, James C., and David W. Gerbing. 1988. “Structural Equation Modeling in Practice: A Review and Recommended Two-Step Approach.” *Psychological Bulletin* 103 (3): 411–423. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.103.3.411.
